intro: Rachmaninoff’s 1911 arrangement of a salon polka was a favourite encore, and this Edison disc of April 1919 is the first of his three disc recordings of it. Follow the tune as the hands trade it, the loud chords, the sudden move to E major, and the quiet close.
question: How does a pianist make a small dance tune sound like a virtuoso piece?

sections.label: Allegretto · the tune over a polka bass
Meno mosso · slowing into a run
Tempo precedente · scherzando in E major
Tempo I · A♭ major returns
sections.mNote: opening tune returns in A♭ at Tempo I

cues.title: A flourish, then the tune
cues.text: The Allegretto opens with a few bars of rising sixteenth-note figures marked mf, dim. and rit. Then, at pp, the tune enters over a left hand that plays a bass note and a chord on each beat: the oom-pah of a polka.
cues.evidence: The Piano Street scan of the 1911 edition shows Allegretto in 2/4, a first system of right-hand sixteenth-note figures with mf, dim. and rit., and a tempo at pp with the tune over a left hand of bass note and chord (https://www.pianostreet.com/rachmaninoff-sheet-music/polka-de-w-r.htm). The analysis shows 6.0 attacks per second at 0:00 falling to 2.2 at 0:05.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: His father’s tune, Behr’s polka
cues.text: The tune was one Rachmaninoff’s father Vasily liked to play, and the title gives his initials. In fact it is Franz Behr’s Lachtäubchen, Op. 303. Rachmaninoff moved it from F to A♭ major and added a new counter-melody for its return.
cues.evidence: Jeremy Nicholas’s note for Hyperion CDA66486 identifies Behr’s Scherzpolka Op. 303, the transposition from F major to A♭ and the added counter-melody: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dw.asp?dc=W5662_GBAJY9148612. IMSLP gives the work as based on Behr’s La Rieuse, Op. 303, published in 1911 and dedicated to Leopold Godowsky: https://imslp.org/wiki/Polka_de_W.R._(Rachmaninoff,_Sergei)

cues.title: A distant piano
cues.text: The 1992 RCA booklet says Edison’s engineer evidently put an upright piano too far from the recording horns, so the results sound “distant and disappointing”. Listen past that distance to the clean articulation of the hands.
cues.evidence: The essay “The Recordings” in the RCA/BMG booklet (1992) describes the upright piano placed too far from the horns: https://archive.org/details/9-0023-sergei-rachmaninoff-complete-recordings-booklet-to-10-cd-set-rca-bmg-09026-61265-2-1992. This describes the Edison sessions in general; it does not single out this take.

cues.title: Louder, with rests between chords
cues.text: Between 0:55 and 1:05 the level rises by about twelve decibels. The score marks Poco più mosso: staccato chords in both hands, then a crescendo to f and ff, with rests between the chord pairs.
cues.evidence: Relative level rises from −20.2 dB at 0:55 to −13.4 dB at 1:00 and −8.5 dB at 1:05; 1:05 and 1:10 are among the five loudest windows, and a boundary of 0.52 falls at 1:04. The score’s third page begins Poco più mosso at mf and reaches f and ff.

cues.title: Ten sides for Edison, in a hurry
cues.text: Rachmaninoff’s first recordings were made for Edison in April 1919. He had arrived in America needing funds, and Edison wanted ten sides at once. Three takes were made of each piece, and Edison issued all three.
cues.evidence: The RCA booklet’s “The Recordings” describes the practical reason for the Edison contract, the ten sides and the three takes each, all issued: https://archive.org/details/9-0023-sergei-rachmaninoff-complete-recordings-booklet-to-10-cd-set-rca-bmg-09026-61265-2-1992. The session date is disputed: the Archive filename and RCA register give 23 April, DAHR’s Edison ledger entry gives 24 April.

cues.title: Scherzando in a new key
cues.text: Near 2:12 the strongest boundary of the record arrives. The score changes to four sharps (E major or C♯ minor) at Tempo precedente, marked scherzando and mf, then returns to A♭ with a rit. and Tempo I.
cues.evidence: Boundaries of 1.00 at 2:12 and 0.97 at 2:16 are the two strongest in the file, and the loudest window is at 2:10 (−6.4 dB). Local key estimates move through B major (2:00) to E major (2:05). The score’s fourth page ends with a double bar and a new signature of four sharps; the fifth page begins Tempo precedente, scherzando.

cues.title: A critic hears the left hand
cues.text: Rachmaninoff played both Lilacs and this polka at Carnegie Hall on 21 December 1918. William James Henderson of The Sun found him “ponderous and staccato with the sinister hand”, yet with “virile vivacity” and “crispness of finger enunciation”.
cues.evidence: The programme and Henderson’s review (The Sun, 22 December 1918) are reproduced in the Classical Pianists chronology: https://classical-pianists.net/vii-b/sergei-rachmaninoff/chronology-2/. “Sinister” is the Latin word for left.

cues.title: The loud final stretch
cues.text: From about 3:25 to 3:50 the record stays loud, with attacks near five a second. The last pages return to A♭ at Tempo I, with fast right-hand figures in the upper octaves and an a tempo con moto.
cues.evidence: Relative level stays between −9.2 and −11.2 dB from 3:25 to 3:50 at 4.8–5.8 attacks per second, and local key estimates favour A♭ major at 3:30–3:45 (r = 0.70–0.79). The score’s seventh and eighth pages show A♭ Tempo I, a tempo con moto and passages in 8va.

cues.title: A soft close
cues.text: The closing bars are Meno mosso, with a ritardando and a last soft chord under a fermata. In this record the level drops at about 3:54, and by 4:05 only a very quiet decay remains.
cues.evidence: A boundary of 0.71 falls at 3:54, the level falls from −11.2 dB at 3:50 to −20.8 dB at 3:55 and −24.2 dB at 4:00, and is −43.8 dB at 4:05 with 1.2 detected attacks per second, so a very quiet decay remains; no exact final release is claimed. The score’s last system is marked Meno mosso, rit. and ends on a chord with a fermata.

transitions.title: Staccato chords speed up and swell
transitions.how: The tune gives way to a faster tempo marked Poco più mosso, still in A♭ major. Both hands play short, accented chords with rests, and a crescendo takes them from mf to f and then ff. The right hand’s decorated tune is replaced by chord pairs that answer each other between the hands, so rhythm and weight change together.
transitions.evidence: Relative level rises from −20.2 dB (0:55) to −8.5 dB (1:05) and a boundary of 0.52 falls at 1:04. The score’s third page begins Poco più mosso at mf. Bar numbers are not assigned.

transitions.title: The loud chords fall away
transitions.how: After the ff chords the score marks a ritardando and Meno mosso. A descending sixteenth-note figure leads into a slower passage at mf with a slurred melodic line over left-hand chords. Tempo and dynamic fall together, and the pages that follow alternate a tempo with further Meno mosso passages.
transitions.evidence: A boundary of 0.85 falls at 1:16, the strongest before the middle of the file, and the level falls from −12.4 dB at 1:15 to −18.4 dB at 1:20. The score’s third page ends with rit. and Meno mosso.

transitions.title: A run into four sharps
transitions.how: The Meno mosso slows poco a poco (rallentando), and the music thins to a lull. Then a veloce run in sextuplets, marked pp and cresc., rises to f and dim. At the double bar the key signature changes to four sharps (E major or C♯ minor) and Tempo precedente restores the opening tempo, marked scherzando and mf. The new key arrives at once, with no pause for modulation.
transitions.evidence: The level falls to −22.9 dB at 1:50 with one attack per second, rises to 7.0 attacks per second at 2:05 and the loudest window of the file at 2:10; boundaries of 1.00 and 0.97 follow at 2:12 and 2:16. Local key estimates move from B major (2:00) to E major (2:05). The score’s fourth page ends with the run and a double bar with four sharps.

transitions.title: Back to A♭ at Tempo I
transitions.how: A double bar ends the scherzando passage in four sharps and returns the key signature to four flats (A♭ major). Forte sextuplet figures over broken chords lead to a ritardando, and Tempo I restores the opening speed at p, with the tune once more over the oom-pah accompaniment. The home key comes back by a change of signature, not through a prepared cadence that the score shows.
transitions.evidence: The score’s fifth page shows the double bar and change of signature back to four flats, f sextuplet figures, rit. and Tempo I at p. Boundaries of 0.73 at 2:34 and 0.61 at 2:38 and a fall in level to −22.7 dB at 2:40 fit the return. Local key estimates are unreliable here; A♭ major is the estimate from 2:50.

transitions.title: Running figures give way to soft chords
transitions.how: The last page adds fast figures in the upper octaves over broken chords, with an a tempo con moto, and a long run rising across the keyboard at pp. Meno mosso then slows the music, with chords in the left hand, a ritardando and a final soft chord under a fermata.
transitions.evidence: A boundary of 0.71 falls at 3:54; level falls from −11.2 dB (3:50) to −20.8 dB (3:55) and −24.2 dB (4:00) and is −43.8 dB at 4:05, with 1.2 detected attacks per second; no exact final release is claimed. The score’s eighth page ends with the pp run, Meno mosso, rit. and a fermata.

fields.label: Work version
fields.value: Composer’s arrangement for piano (1911) of Franz Behr’s Scherzpolka Lachtäubchen, Op. 303, as played by him
fields.note: The printed title is Polka de W. R. (W. for Wassily, the composer’s father); the RCA set and the Archive file use V.R. Behr’s theme is transposed from F to A♭ with an added counter-melody and without Behr’s middle section. The score prints ossia alternatives, and the edition used by the composer for this recording is not identified.

fields.label: Recorded
fields.note: Sources agree on April 1919 and disagree on the day. The Archive filenames, the RCA register give 23 April; DAHR’s Edison ledger entry and the Classical Pianists chronology give 24 April. The day is not resolved here.

fields.label: Place
fields.note: DAHR gives New York for every take. The label place of publication, Orange, New Jersey, is not the session place.

fields.label: Label
fields.note: Edison is the original label (released at Orange, New Jersey, according to DAHR’s label record); the uploader identifies the 1992 RCA/BMG set as the immediate source of the file.

fields.label: Catalogue
fields.value: Edison Diamond Disc 82187 (10-inch double-faced; Polka on side L, Prelude in C♯ minor on side R); RCA-BMG 09026 61265 2, CD 10 (1992)
fields.note: The side assignment and disc number are documented by the Edison list and the Florida Atlantic catalogue; the disc used for the 1992 transfer is not identified. DAHR’s MARC record for the disc gives 10-inch, 80 rpm and a bracketed publication year of [1919], which predates the release documented by the National Park Service and Densmore (December 1920) and is not followed for the release date; either proposed publication year predates 1926.

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides
fields.note: The RCA register names Edison 6744-B for CD 10, track 15, and the Archive file is that track. Edison issued all three takes (A, B, C) on the same catalogue number, so the disc number alone does not identify the take, and no comparison of takes was made. DAHR gives its own take dates (24 April 1919) which differ from the RCA register (23 April).

fields.label: Transfer
fields.value: John Pfeiffer, reissue producer; Ward Marston, disc-to-DAT transfer; André Gauthier, remastering supervisor; Anthony Salvatore, remastering engineer
fields.note: These are the credits printed for the 1992 RCA/BMG set. Their connection to this access file rests on the uploader’s identification of the item as CD 10 of that set. The later ripper and uploader are not named as engineers.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: The set was issued in 1992, but the dates of the disc-to-DAT transfer, the remastering and the later CD extraction are not stated. The Internet Archive upload of 11 October 2025 is not a transfer date.

fields.label: Processing
fields.value: Disc-to-DAT transfer, then digital remastering at BMG/RCA Studios, New York City; the Internet Archive derives its VBR MP3 from an uploaded WAV.
fields.note: The booklet says surface imperfections were reduced without radical removal of all surface noise. It gives no equalisation, pitch-correction, noise-reduction or editing settings, and none is inferred from the audio analysis. The booklet’s essay says the Edison engineer evidently placed the upright piano too far from the recording horns, so the sound is distant.

fields.label: Composition rights
fields.value: Underlying composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies.
fields.note: Rachmaninoff died in 1943. This is a territorial term calculation, not worldwide clearance or a statement about any modern edition. Franz Behr died in 1898, so the underlying polka is also out of copyright on the same calculation.

fields.label: Recording rights
fields.value: US public domain: the issued sound recording was published by 1925 (Edison Diamond Disc 82187, released December 1920).
fields.note: The National Park Service catalogue and Densmore’s list both give a December 1920 release for Edison 82187, whose side L carries the Polka; this is independent of the April 1919 session date. The Archive item’s Public Domain Mark is noted but not relied on. The 1992 booklet carries an all-rights-reserved reissue notice: no claim is made that its text, artwork or compilation is public domain, or that any new creative contribution to the mastering is cleared worldwide.

quote.text: I feel like a ghost wandering in a world grown alien. I cannot cast out the old way of writing, and I cannot acquire the new.
quote.source: Interview with Leonard Liebling, The Musical Courier, 1939

composer.background:
Rachmaninoff learnt the sound of Russian worship before he learnt orchestration. His grandmother took him to Orthodox services, where unaccompanied voices and bells occupied different parts of the ceremony: chant inside the church, metal sounding above and outside it. His music repeatedly brings the two together. A melody moves in narrow steps while bass notes toll beneath it; a chord is struck again before its previous resonance has died. The C♯ minor Prelude, the Second Piano Concerto and The Bells make this audible without requiring an actual church bell. The All-Night Vigil removes the instruments altogether, leaving a choir to produce both the sustained line and the accumulating weight of the harmony.

Born into a landowning family in 1873, he spent his early childhood at Oneg, near Novgorod. His father’s financial failures brought the sale of the estates and a move to St Petersburg. Rachmaninoff entered its Conservatory in 1883, but his general schoolwork deteriorated; his parents separated, and his sister Sofia died of diphtheria. In 1885 his cousin Alexander Siloti recommended a transfer to Moscow and the supervision of Nikolai Zverev. The move exchanged a disorganised household for one in which practice, meals and attendance at concerts were regulated by a piano teacher.
composer.epithet: A composer-pianist who built long melodies over tolling basses, and carried Russian chant into the concertos and dances of his American exile.
